```{r Original Model}
source("data_cleaning.R", echo = FALSE)
source("helper_functions.R", echo = FALSE)
```

We sought to fix model assumptions. Log (ln(x+1)) transform was conducted on right skewed data, and log transform was conducted on the LBFDGHPW (hours worked per week) reflected by the max value to prevent negative values. 

```{r skew-correcting-original-model}
original_predictors <- c(
  "PAADVVOL", 
  "PAA_15A",
  "LBFDGHPW",
  "GEN_05",
  "GEN_01",
  "GEN_10",
  "INCDGHH",
  "EDDVH3",
  "FSCDVHF2",
  "DHH_SEX"
)

original_model_data <- get_model_data(cleaned_data, original_predictors, "LSM_01")

original_model <- lm(
  formula = LSM_01 ~ PAADVVOL * GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 + INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX,
  data = original_model_data
)

# handing skewness of the numerical predictors
skew_corrected_model_data <- original_model_data

# fitting new model with transformed preds.
# PAADVVOL, PAA_15A is right skewed
# LBFDGHPW is left skewed
c_val <- max(original_model_data$LBFDGHPW) + 1 # for log(c-x) transformation to handel left skew
skew_corrected_model_data$PAADVVOL <- log1p(original_model_data$PAADVVOL)
skew_corrected_model_data$PAA_15A <- log1p(original_model_data$PAA_15A)
skew_corrected_model_data$LBFDGHPW <- log(c_val - (original_model_data$LBFDGHPW))

skew_corrected_model <- lm(
  formula = LSM_01 ~ PAADVVOL * GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 + INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX,
  data = skew_corrected_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  skew_corrected_model, 
  original_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/skew_corrected_model", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(original_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = skew_corrected_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  original_model, 
  original_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/original_model", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(original_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = original_model_data
)
```

This seemed to correct the skews of the predictors well. However, the evidence of model assumption violations were still present. Next, the response (Life Satisfaction) was transformed using BoxCox transformation. A lambda value of around 2 was found, and thus a square transform was conducted. Normality was largely corrected and linearity left intact, but heteroskedasticity was still present. 

```{r boxcox-transformation-of-original-model}
library(car)

# Fitting Y + 1 to prevent log(0) errors
boxcox_fit <- lm(
  I(LSM_01 + 1) ~ PAADVVOL * GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 +
    INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX,
  data = skew_corrected_model_data
)

# Finding optimization for normalizing errors
summary(powerTransform(boxcox_fit))

boxcox_model_data <- skew_corrected_model_data

boxcox_model_data$LSM_01 <- (skew_corrected_model_data$LSM_01 + 1)^2

boxcox_model <- lm(
  formula = LSM_01 ~ PAADVVOL * GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 + INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX,
  data = boxcox_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  boxcox_model, 
  original_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/boxcox_model", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(original_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = boxcox_model_data
)
```

Tried dropping PAA_15A and see how the plots look like. This didn't work (The code can be found in previous iterations on the Github). 

Without transformations, the residual plots look to same. Now I will try to fix boxcox on the predictors instead (goal here is I don't want to transform response because I feel like the interpreting that would be hard). This also didn't work (the code can be found in previous iterations on the Gitub). 

After checking the plots, this didn't do anything. So we decided to keep the old method of fixing assumptions.

Next, we wanted to remove predictors to improve our model fit. We first compared two baseline models: 
- Reduced Model: Predicts self-reported life satisfaction (`LSM_01`) using main effects only.
- Full Model: Adds an interaction term between physical activity volume (`PAADVVOL`) and perceived mental health (`GEN_05`) to test whether the effect of physical activity depends on mental health status.

```{r testing-interaction-term}
# Fit Reduced Model 
model_reduced <- lm(
  LSM_01 ~ PAADVVOL + GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 + 
    INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX,
  data = boxcox_model_data
)

# Partial F Test comparing the interaction term
anova(model_reduced, boxcox_model)
```

The partial F test produces a high p-value (close to 1), indicating that the interaction term does not significantly improve model fit. However, since this interaction term is critical to our research question, it will be kept. To justify our choice of which predictors we decided to drop, we will do an All Possible Subsets of Model Selection method using both adj_R2 and BIC as readouts. 

Note that we will continue using the data subsetted to all original predictors (`r nrow(original_model_data` observations), even when predictors are being removed to maintain consistency. 

```{r all possible subsets model selection}
# install.packages("leaps")
library(leaps)
best <- regsubsets(LSM_01 ~ PAADVVOL * GEN_05 + PAA_15A + LBFDGHPW + GEN_01 + GEN_10 + 
    INCDGHH + EDDVH3 + FSCDVHF2 + DHH_SEX, data = boxcox_model_data, nbest = 2, nvmax = 11, really.big = TRUE, method = "exhaustive")
# nvmax default is 8, really.big is needed above 9 preds
summary(best)

#plotting for visualization
# note: with subsets(best, statistic = "adjr2",legend = FALSE) everything was overlapping and impossible to read
```

```{r all-possible-subsets-plot, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}
# create the output folder if it doesn't exist
out_dir <- "part_two/figures/all_possible_subsets_selection"
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# helper: regsubsets plot with smaller, 30-degree-tilted variable labels
plot_rs <- function(fit, scale, main, label_cex = 0.7, angle = 30) {
  labs <- c("(Intercept)", fit$xnames[-1])
  plot(fit, scale = scale, main = main, labels = rep("", length(labs)))
  usr <- par("usr")
  text(x = seq_along(labs),
       y = usr[3] - 0.02 * (usr[4] - usr[3]),
       labels = labs, srt = angle, adj = 1, xpd = TRUE, cex = label_cex)
}

# draw the two panels (wrapped in a function so we can reuse it)
plot_subsets <- function() {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(12, 4, 3, 1), cex.axis = 0.7)
  on.exit(par(op))
  plot_rs(best, "adjr2", "Adjusted R²")
  plot_rs(best, "bic",   "BIC")
}

# save to file
png(file.path(out_dir, "all_possible_subsets_selection.png"),
    width = 14, height = 8, units = "in", res = 300)
plot_subsets()
invisible(dev.off())

# also show it in the knitted document
plot_subsets()
```

Resulting subsetted model. From the plot after conducting all possible subsets selection, if we look at the BIC, it can be seen that the model with the highest adjR2 includes our interaction term and PAADVVOL, as well as DHH_SEX. We also see that a model with very low BIC also includes the interaction term PAADVVOL:GEN_05 (we care about this term since it is our research question). Thus, we will keep the following predictors:
- PAADVVOL (critical for research question)
- GEN_05 (critical for research question)
- GEN_01
- GEN_10
- DHH_SEX
- PAADVVOL:GEN_05 (critical for research question)

```{r subsetted-model}
library(lmtest)
library(car)
new_relevant_predictors <- c("PAADVVOL", "GEN_05", "GEN_01", "GEN_10", "DHH_SEX")

subsetted_model_data <- get_model_data(cleaned_data, new_relevant_predictors, "LSM_01")

subsetted_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_relevant_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "LSM_01"),
  data = subsetted_model_data
)

# 1. Multicollinearity (VIF)
vif(subsetted_model, type = "predictor") # added "type" parameter since we have an interaction term.

# 2. Residual Diagnostic Plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(subsetted_model, main = "Subsetted Model Diagnostics")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# 3. Coefficient Summary
coeftest(subsetted_model, vcov = hccm(subsetted_model, type = "hc3"))
```

The same skew-corrections and boxcox transformation procedure will be applied to correct normality. 

Note on interpretting GVIF:
because we have an interaction term we cant use normal vif (the VIFs change depending on which level we choose as the baseline). Instead, we have to use GVIF which captures the volume of similarity between models. But since its a volume it grows with dimensions so we have to look at GVIF^(1/(2*Df)). to compare it to the cutoff of 5 or 10 we have to square the GVIF^(1/(2*Df)).

```{r subsetted model: skew correction}
# handing skewness of the numerical predictors
skew_corrected_subsetted_model_data <- subsetted_model_data

# fitting new model with transformed preds.
# PAADVVOL is right skewed
skew_corrected_subsetted_model_data$PAADVVOL <- log1p(subsetted_model_data$PAADVVOL)

skew_corrected_subsetted_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_relevant_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), "LSM_01"),
  data = skew_corrected_subsetted_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  skew_corrected_subsetted_model, 
  new_relevant_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/subsetted_model_skew_corrected", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_relevant_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = skew_corrected_subsetted_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  subsetted_model, 
  new_relevant_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/subsetted_model", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_relevant_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = subsetted_model_data
)
```

```{r subsetted model: response transformation}
library(car)

boxcox_subsetted_model_data <- skew_corrected_subsetted_model_data

# Fitting Y + 1 to prevent log(0) errors
subsetted_boxcox_fit <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_relevant_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "I(LSM_01 + 1)"),
  data = boxcox_subsetted_model_data
)

# Finding optimization for normalizing errors
summary(powerTransform(subsetted_boxcox_fit))

boxcox_subsetted_model_data$LSM_01 <- (boxcox_subsetted_model_data$LSM_01 + 1)^2

boxcox_subsetted_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_relevant_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), "LSM_01"),
  data = boxcox_subsetted_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  boxcox_subsetted_model, 
  new_relevant_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/subsetted_model_boxcox", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_relevant_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = boxcox_subsetted_model_data
)

# Visualizing standardized plots
generate_plots(
  boxcox_subsetted_model, 
  new_relevant_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/subsetted_model_boxcox_standardized", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_relevant_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = boxcox_subsetted_model_data,
  standardized = TRUE
)

summary(boxcox_subsetted_model)
```

To think about which predictors to add, we will first identify problematic points. The pattern of these points may highlight a missing predictor in our model. 

```{r identifying-problematic-points}
p <- length(coef(boxcox_subsetted_model)) - 1 # Number of predictors
n <- nobs(boxcox_subsetted_model) # Number of observations

# Outliers
ri <- rstandard(boxcox_subsetted_model)

outliers_indices <- which(abs(ri) > 4)

# Leverage points
hii <- hatvalues(boxcox_subsetted_model)

leverage_point_indices <- which(hii > 2*(p+1)/n)

# Influential Points: Cooks distance 
cooks_distances <- cooks.distance(boxcox_subsetted_model)

cooks_problematic_point_indices <- which(cooks_distances > qf(0.5, p + 1, n - p - 1))

# Influential Points: DFFITS
dffits <- dffits(boxcox_subsetted_model)

dffits_problematic_point_indices <- which(abs(dffits) > 2*sqrt((p+1) / n))

# Influential Points: DFBETAS
dfbetas <- dfbetas(boxcox_subsetted_model)
num_bad_betas <- rowSums(1*(abs(dfbetas) > 2 / sqrt(n)))

cat("Num outliers:", length(outliers_indices), "\n")
cat("Num leverage points:", length(leverage_point_indices), "\n\n")
cat("Number of problematic points determined using:\n")
cat("Cooks:", length(cooks_problematic_point_indices), "\n")
cat("DFFITS:", length(dffits_problematic_point_indices), "\n")
cat("DFBETAS:", sum(1*(num_bad_betas > 0)), "\n")
```

Goal: Improve model fit while decreasing residuals of problematic points. I will test the addition of every possible predictor, and read three specific outputs: 
1. How much the adjusted R2 value increases
2. How much the residuals of each problematic point drops
3. How much the residuals of each non-problematic point drops. 

We want predictors where all three hold:
- R2 value remains constant or increases
- residuals of each problematic point drops significantly
- residuals of non-problematic points don't get higher. 

```{r testing-every-new-predictor}
current_predictors <- attr(terms(boxcox_subsetted_model), "term.labels")
candidate_predictors <- setdiff(non_NA, c(current_predictors, "LSM_01"))

temp_model_data <- cleaned_data |>
  drop_na(any_of(c(current_predictors, "LSM_01")))

# Transforming temporary data

temp_model_data$LSM_01   <- (temp_model_data$LSM_01 + 1)^2
temp_model_data$PAADVVOL <- log1p(temp_model_data$PAADVVOL)

# Problematic points in a model: flagged by DFFITS or an outlier (|r_i| > 4)
problematic_points <- function(m) {
  n_m <- nobs(m)
  p_m <- length(coef(m)) - 1
  abs(dffits(m)) > 2 * sqrt((p_m + 1) / n_m) | abs(rstandard(m)) > 4
}

candidate_results <- lapply(candidate_predictors, FUN = function(pred) {

  relevant_model_data <- temp_model_data |>
    drop_na(any_of(pred))

  if (nrow(relevant_model_data) < 1000) return(NULL)

  # Current model and current model + candidate, fitted on the same rows
  og_model <- lm(reformulate(current_predictors, response = "LSM_01"), data = relevant_model_data)
  model <- tryCatch(
    lm(reformulate(c(current_predictors, pred), response = "LSM_01"), data = relevant_model_data),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(model)) return(NULL)

  flagged <- problematic_points(og_model) # problematic before adding the candidate
  e_old <- abs(resid(og_model)) # how far off each prediction was
  e_new <- abs(resid(model)) # how far off it is with the candidate added

  tibble(
    predictor = pred,
    description = dict[[pred]],
    n = nobs(model),
    n_flagged = sum(flagged),
    gain_in_adj_r2 = summary(model)$adj.r.squared - summary(og_model)$adj.r.squared,
    
    # % reduction in average |residual|, for flagged points 
    pct_resid_drop_flagged = 100 * (1 - mean(e_new[flagged])  / mean(e_old[flagged])),

    # % reduction in average |residual| for all other points
    pct_resid_drop_others  = 100 * (1 - mean(e_new[!flagged]) / mean(e_old[!flagged]))
  )

}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  arrange(desc(pct_resid_drop_flagged))

candidate_results

```

From this analysis, satisfaction with life in general (LSMDVSWL) as a predictor came up as the best. However, this is a grouped version of our response (i.e. derived from response). Therefore, it is not an appropriate predictor and will be ignored. 

However, the following predictors seemed promising (increased adjR2, decreased avg residual of problematic points by at least 1%, and also decreased avg residuals of other points):
- SLP_015 (Frequency of refreshing sleep)
- GEN_20 (sense of belonging to local community)
- COV2_005 (Self-perceived mental health before / after the pandemic)
- DHHDGHSZ (Yes = Lives alone, No = Lives with others)
- SLP_010 (Trouble going to sleep or staying asleep - frequency)

For each of these, we will determine whether we see an improvement to AIC. Here we are using AIC (not BIC from before) since we are not concerned with having a simpler model, as we have already subsetted the predictors greatly and are more confident in our choices. Thus, we will compute AIC for each subset. 

Note that we did not do forward selection: This is because we are interested in inference regarding exercise, mental health, and life satisfaction. By restricting our model choices to a few candidate predictors, and carefully evaluating each one, we can maintain prioritization of inference while attaining a good and robust model that is not missing necessary predictors. 

```{r fitting-new-model}
new_added_predictors <- c(new_relevant_predictors, "SLP_015", "GEN_20", "COV2_005", "DHHDGHSZ", "SLP_010")

new_model_data <- get_model_data(cleaned_data, new_added_predictors, response = "LSM_01")
new_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "LSM_01"),
  data = new_model_data
)

summary(new_model)
```

Off the bat, this added quite a few predictors that were significant. Keep in mind this does not include transformed variables, so model assumptions will need to be re-assessed. 

In particular, living alone, perceived mental health before vs after pandemic, sense of belonging to local community, and frequency of refreshing sleep came up as significant predictors.


```{r subset-selection-on-new-model}
# install.packages("leaps")
library(leaps)
best <- regsubsets(
  x = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "LSM_01"), 
  data = new_model_data, 
  nbest = 2, 
  nvmax = 11, really.big = TRUE, method = "exhaustive")
# nvmax default is 8, really.big is needed above 9 preds
summary(best)

#plotting for visualization
# note: with subsets(best, statistic = "adjr2",legend = FALSE) everything was overlapping and impossible to read
```

```{r subset-selection-on-new-model-plots, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}
# create the output folder if it doesn't exist
out_dir <- "part_two/figures/all_possible_subsets_selection"
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# helper: regsubsets plot with smaller, 30-degree-tilted variable labels
plot_rs <- function(fit, scale, main, label_cex = 0.7, angle = 30) {
  labs <- c("(Intercept)", fit$xnames[-1])

  usr <- par("usr")
  text(x = seq_along(labs),
       y = usr[3] - 0.02 * (usr[4] - usr[3]),
       labels = labs, srt = angle, adj = 1, xpd = TRUE, cex = label_cex)
}

# draw the two panels (wrapped in a function so we can reuse it)

  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(12, 4, 3, 1), cex.axis = 0.7)
```

Here, we find that the model with SLP_010 is not great. Thus, we will remove SLP_010 from the final model. The original metrics PAADVVOL (physical activity) and the interaction term with GEN_05 were still not significant. This may change after correcting model assumptions. 

```{r fitting-new-fixed-model}
new_added_predictors <- c(new_relevant_predictors, "SLP_015", "GEN_20", "COV2_005", "DHHDGHSZ")

new_model_data <- get_model_data(cleaned_data, new_added_predictors, response = "LSM_01")
new_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "LSM_01"),
  data = new_model_data
)

summary(new_model)
```

Now, we will check assumptions again.

```{r visualizing-assumptions}
generate_plots(new_model, relevant_predictors = new_added_predictors[!grepl(":", new_added_predictors)], output_dir = "part_two/figures/new_model", pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_added_predictors, numeric_classes), model_data = new_model_data)
```

This shows violation of normality. Thus, Boxcox will be performed on the response in the same way as above. The right-skew for PAADVVOL will also be corrected in the same way as above. All other predictors are discrete in nature and so they will not be skew-corrected. 

```{r}
boxcox_new_model_data <- new_model_data

# fitting new model with transformed preds.
# PAADVVOL is right skewed
boxcox_new_model_data$PAADVVOL <- log1p(boxcox_new_model_data$PAADVVOL)

# Fitting Y + 1 to prevent log(0) errors
new_boxcox_fit <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "I(LSM_01 + 1)"),
  data = boxcox_new_model_data
)

# Finding optimization for normalizing errors
summary(powerTransform(new_boxcox_fit))

boxcox_new_model_data$LSM_01 <- (boxcox_new_model_data$LSM_01 + 1)^2

boxcox_new_model <- lm(
  formula = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), "LSM_01"),
  data = boxcox_new_model_data
)

generate_plots(
  boxcox_new_model, 
  new_added_predictors, 
  output_dir = "part_two/figures/new_model_boxcox", 
  pairwise_predictors = intersect(new_added_predictors, numeric_classes), 
  model_data = boxcox_new_model_data
)
```

This fixed normality, and variance seems to be relatively constant. Assumptions seem to hold well. However, the interaction term and PAADVVOL term remained not significant. To see if we can remove any more predictors with the transformed model, we checked all subsets one last time. 

```{r subset-selection-on-final-model}
# install.packages("leaps")
library(leaps)
best <- regsubsets(
  x = reformulate(c(new_added_predictors, "PAADVVOL:GEN_05"), response = "LSM_01"), 
  data = boxcox_new_model_data, 
  nbest = 2, 
  nvmax = 11, really.big = TRUE, method = "exhaustive")
# nvmax default is 8, really.big is needed above 9 preds
summary(best)

#plotting for visualization
# note: with subsets(best, statistic = "adjr2",legend = FALSE) everything was overlapping and impossible to read
```

```{r subset-selection-on-final-model-plots, fig.width=14, fig.height=8}

dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# helper: regsubsets plot with smaller, 30-degree-tilted variable labels
plot_rs <- function(fit, scale, main, label_cex = 0.7, angle = 30) {
  labs <- c("(Intercept)", fit$xnames[-1])
  plot(fit, scale = scale, main = main, labels = rep("", length(labs)))
  usr <- par("usr")
  text(x = seq_along(labs),
       y = usr[3] - 0.02 * (usr[4] - usr[3]),
       labels = labs, srt = angle, adj = 1, xpd = TRUE, cex = label_cex)
}

# draw the two panels (wrapped in a function so we can reuse it)
plot_subsets <- function() {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(12, 4, 3, 1), cex.axis = 0.7)
  on.exit(par(op))
  plot_rs(best, "adjr2", "Adjusted R²")

```

This confirms that removing PAADVVOL and our interaction term are the only actions that will decrease (improve) the AIC, suggesting that the other predictors are important. We keep the latter as they are the focus of our research question.

We will not perform forward selection to pick new predictors. Since we are particularly interested in inference and not prediction, we will maintain a simpler and interpretable model rather than applying greedy algorithms to get the best model.

Before we conclude our final models, check about multicolinearity one last time.
```{r}
vif(boxcox_new_model, type = "predictor")
```
From the results, nothing is violated. Thus, this concludes our final model. In this model, PAADVVOL and our interaction term were not found to be siginificant predictors of life satisfaction. 

```{r final-summary-output}
summary(boxcox_new_model)
```

Notes:
Interestingly, frequency of refreshing sleep (SLP_015) is strongly and significantly associated with perceived life satisfaction. It is known that both exercise and mental health impact frequency of refreshing sleep. It would be interesting to explore the dynamics between mental health, exercise, and refreshing sleep.
